_: THE MUST-REFUSE CORPUS. Every case here MUST be refused by the closed table. The census over it (`tools/ast_conformance.py --escapes`) is the D-phase analogue of C's repaint oracle, pointing the other way: C's oracle had to read NON-ZERO on the unmodified tree; this one has to read ZERO on the GUARDED interpreter, so a zero here proves nothing on its own and the run aborts unless the SAME corpus through the UNGUARDED interpreter reads non-zero.
_shape: `ast` is the JSEP tree -- the parser's output, NOT the canonical persisted tree. That is deliberate: the table closes at the parse->canonical boundary, so a corpus written in canonical shape could not express the escapes at all (a MemberExpression has no canonical form). `source` is what a user would type.
_parses: Each case must PARSE before it proves anything about the interpreter. A case the parser rejects says nothing about what the tree walker would have done, and `member_access` is exactly where that bites -- jsep parses `a.b` happily. Every case here is declared `parses: true`, which is the CONSERVATIVE direction: if Task 3's configured jsep refuses one of them outright it moves to PARSER_REFUSED and the escape total goes DOWN, never up. Task 3 owes the first real measurement of this field.
_disjointness: The brief asked for a disjoint fragment PER CASE; that is measurably wrong for this corpus and the deviation is deliberate. C Task 9's defect was two DIFFERENT GATES sharing a phrase, so `raises(match=...)` still matched with one gate deleted. Two cases refused by the SAME gate for the SAME reason legitimately share a message. So each case names its `guard`, and the rail is stricter than per-case disjointness: two cases share a fragment IFF they share a guard, and no fragment from one guard may be a substring of a fragment from another.
_fragment_matching: The per-case `refuse` fragment is ARMED, not yet enforced: nothing refuses anything today because no guarded pipeline exists. It is enforced the first time `tools/ast_conformance.py --escapes` finds a guard (Task 6). Until then the census asserts only PARSED-then-NOT-REFUSED, which is what makes today's number honest.

cases.refuse: `this` names nothing this table can resolve
cases.why: `this` is a binding the interpreter supplies, not a name the user declared, so it is the one identifier whose value depends on HOW the walker was called rather than on the table

cases.refuse: only a bare table name may be called
cases.why: a callee that is an EXPRESSION rather than a name. Every table entry is reached by name; the moment a computed value can occupy the callee slot, the set of callable things stops being the table

cases.refuse: array literals have no meaning in a column formula
cases.why: a column formula produces one value per bar; an array literal produces a container, which is a second kind of value the table has no rule for
cases.note: this tree contains BOTH an ArrayExpression and a MemberExpression, so whichever guard the canonicaliser reaches first decides the MESSAGE. The case declares the array guard because a canonicaliser that recurses into `object` before deciding meets the array first. If Task 3's canonicaliser refuses the member first, that is a finding for Task 3 to reconcile in this file -- the case is REFUSED either way, so the census number does not move.

cases.refuse: a formula produces a column; it does not bind a name
cases.why: assignment introduces STATE, and a stateful formula's value at bar i can depend on the order the walker visited bars -- which is the property the repaint linter's whole analysis assumes away
cases.note: MEASURED BY TASK 3, 2026-08-07, AND THE DECLARATION MOVED: jsep 1.4.0's core grammar has no assignment operator (it ships as a plugin), and `jsep('x = 1')` throws `Unexpected "=" at character 2`. So this case is PARSER_REFUSED and `parses` is now `false`. The escape census therefore reads 15 of 16, not 16 of 16 -- Task 2 declared `parses: true` as the conservative direction (over-counting an escape is the safe way to be wrong) and wrote that a case moving to PARSER_REFUSED makes the total go DOWN. It went down. That is a CORRECTION, not a regression, and Task 6 still owes the first zero. The `guard` and `ast` below are kept: the day an assignment plugin is loaded the case must be a canonicalise refusal, and `parse.js` implements that guard and exercises it directly.

the same prototype reach through a different member, so a guard that special-cased `toString` by name is caught here. Shares `prototype_name`'s guard by design -- one lookup rule refuses every Object.prototype member at once
a name that is not on the scope object at all and resolves through the SCOPE CHAIN in a naive walker. `globalThis` is one identifier away from every API the browser has

the ordinary case: a well-formed call to a name that is not in the table. Distinct from `resolve:name` because the callee slot is resolved against `functions`, not against `series` -- two dictionaries, and a walker that consulted one union would accept `close(3)`

a KNOWN name called wrongly. In JS a missing argument is `undefined` and `sma(close)` would return a column of NaN; in Python it is a TypeError. That is a cross-lane divergence produced by the ABSENCE of a check, which is the shape no golden fixture can carry

the tree is generated rather than typed because 4,000 nodes cannot be hand-written and a generated SHAPE is not a generated ORACLE -- the assertion is still hand-declared. An unbudgeted walker either blows the stack or takes the request thread with it, and both are denial of service from a text box
a single argument asking for more history than exists. Cheap to write, unbounded to compute, and it passes every node-count budget

Its names are GENERATED FROM THE MANIFEST rather than typed, so a series rename cannot quietly turn this into a `resolve:name` case at a different door.
cases.note: ⭐ THE CAP COUNTS DISTINCT READS, and this case is what proves it is not a latch nothing can trip. ⚰️ THIS SAID *"The cap counts OCCURRENCES, not distinct names, and that is forced rather than stylistic: the table declares FIVE series, so a distinct-name count could never exceed 8 and `budget:series` would be a latch nothing can trip. This case therefore repeats four of the five."* — and the ARGUMENT was sound on the day it was written. Its PREMISE expired: the scalars section landed afterwards, a scalar rides the same `series` node, and the manifest now declares 59 names a definition can read rather than five. So a distinct count has room to exceed eight, and this case does it with nine. ⛔ WHY IT HAD TO CHANGE: counting occurrences refused formulas that read three columns and mentioned them six times — `(high + low + close) / 3` compared against its own average is the whole example — and the cap’s own rationale is DATA VOLUME, which is a function of distinct columns. What surfaced it was the Pine built-in `tr` expanding to six references over three series, which made a real published ATR script translate and then refuse AT THE SAVE DOOR. The cap did not move; only what it measures did, and distinct <= occurrences always.

cases.why: THE CASE A PER-ARGUMENT LOOKBACK CHECK MISSES. Neither 5000 alone need exceed a budget; the tree's lookback is the SUM along the path, which is the same arithmetic Task 7's repaint linter depends on. A guard that checked each call in isolation passes this and nothing else in the corpus catches it

THE OTHER HALF OF THE SCALAR PARTITION, MADE A REFUSAL. `snapshot_date` IS a real column of `screener_rows` and it is in `_scalars_excluded` -- it is an as-of SOURCE, so declaring it would let a formula compute on its own freshness stamp. Naming it must land in exactly the same place as a name nobody ever heard of. Shares `resolve:name` and its fragment with the three cases above BY DESIGN: one mechanism refuses all five, and demanding five different messages would be demanding five gates where one is correct

THE EXCLUSION A USER WILL ACTUALLY REACH FOR. `sector` is a screener column and it is TEXT, and this table's only literal is a number (`_booleans`) -- so `sector == "Technology"` is not merely undeclared, it is INEXPRESSIBLE, and granting it means string literals in the parser, both interpreters, the linter and the read-back. Until that decision is taken the name must refuse, and this case is what goes red the day somebody adds a TEXT column to `scalars` to make a demo work
